overview: This file brings together occupation-era assessments of two Japanese pharmaceutical industries: penicillin and vitamin oils. An August 1947 War Department letter forwards consultant Jackson W. Foster’s May 1947 report on the prospects for Japanese penicillin production, emphasizing tank-process development, reuse of idle industrial equipment, raw-material requirements, costs, and obstacles to large-scale manufacture. A February 1949 despatch from the U.S. Political Adviser in Tokyo forwards a Hypothec Bank of Japan study documenting the recovery of the vitamin-oil industry, its factories, production methods, exports, supply bottlenecks, prices, and manufacturers; the enclosed bank periodical also contains an article on Japanese bank credit and economic reconstruction.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding Foster’s report on Japanese penicillin production
subfiles.from: Ray J. Laux, War Department Special Staff, Civil Affairs Division
subfiles.to: Warde M. Cameron, Department of State
subfiles.about: Forwards the report prepared by penicillin consultant Jackson W. Foster in response to a State Department request transmitted to SCAP.
subfiles.summary: Laux recalls War Department radio W 88343 of May 18, 1946, requesting an expert assessment of Japanese penicillin production. He reports that SCAP supplied Foster’s conclusions on August 1, 1947, and encloses a copy for the Department of State.

subfiles.title: Foster report on Japanese penicillin production
subfiles.about: Assesses the facilities, raw materials, processes, costs, and timetable for establishing large-scale penicillin production in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The report finds that Japan had no pre-existing mass-production facilities and only about twenty small surface-process plants, while approximately ten tank-process pilot plants were expected within three to six months. Foster argues that idle or bomb-damaged heavy-industrial facilities could provide most equipment, although specialized freeze-drying vacuum pumps and precision instruments might require importation. He analyzes media ingredients and extraction chemicals, recommends maximizing yield even at comparatively low potency, and suggests that salvaged equipment and low labor costs could make Japanese penicillin inexpensive. Contamination, raw-material availability, investment uncertainty, coal allocation, and fear of competition from imported American penicillin remained major obstacles; large-scale output was estimated to be eighteen to twenty-four months away under favorable conditions.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 85 forwarding a report on Japan’s vitamin-oil industry
subfiles.from: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards five copies of a Hypothec Bank of Japan report and summarizes the revival, output, and exports of Japan’s vitamin-oil industry.
subfiles.summary: The despatch warns that the enclosed report contains statistical inconsistencies but considers it useful to the Departments of State and Commerce. It notes that production peaked at 450,800 kilograms in 1940, recovered sharply in 1947, and reportedly reached 427,400 kilograms in 1948. Production performance varied by oil type, while postwar exports—especially to the United States—were increasing.

subfiles.title: HBJ Research Monthly No. 8: Vitamin Oil Industry and Credit Situation in Japan
subfiles.from: Hypothec Bank of Japan (Nippon Kangyo Bank)
subfiles.about: Surveys Japan’s vitamin-oil industry and, in a second article, the distribution of Japanese bank credit during postwar reconstruction.
subfiles.summary: The principal study traces commercial vitamin-oil production from cod-liver-oil manufacture on Rebun Island in 1888 through the industry’s prewar expansion, wartime decline, and postwar recovery. Detailed tables cover output by year and fish species, government production targets, factory distribution and capacity, pressure and alkali extraction methods, exports, raw-material rationing, prices, leading manufacturers, and trade organizations. The report presents fish-liver shortages, inadequate finance, black-market purchases, obsolete equipment, and reduced fishing grounds as the chief constraints, while portraying American demand as the basis for substantial future exports. The final pages contain a separate article showing that postwar bank lending favored mining, manufacturing, power, and transportation, followed by publication information for the HBJ Research Monthly.

interest: The file juxtaposes an American technical consultant’s assessment with a Japanese bank’s promotional industrial survey, allowing historians to compare occupation authorities’ expectations with Japanese industry’s own account of recovery. Foster’s report is especially useful for its unusually concrete discussion of converting bomb-damaged or idle industrial equipment to pharmaceutical production and of deliberately balancing potency against total yield. The vitamin-oil report supplies rare factory-level, regional, production, price, and export data, while the covering despatch candidly flags contradictions in those statistics. The appended credit article also places pharmaceutical and export-industry reconstruction within the broader allocation of scarce postwar finance.
